answer: The crisis was sparked by the U.S. housing-price decline and poor-quality mortgages that were bundled into opaque securities; when prices fell, defaults rose, banks held uncertain securities, and on September 15, 2008 Lehman Brothers went bankrupt, turning a financial crisis into a global economic crisis.

Economists care about unemployment because of its direct effect on the welfare of the unemployed (financial and psychological suffering) and because it signals that the economy may not be using its resources efficiently / may be below potential.
They use real GDP (output measured at common/base-year prices) rather than nominal GDP, so measured growth reflects changes in quantities rather than price changes.

In 2009 average growth in advanced economies was -3.7%, by far the lowest annual growth rate since the Great Depression; emerging and developing economies stayed positive but grew nearly 4 percentage points slower than their 2000-2007 average. Stock prices lost half or more of their value from previous peaks.
U.S. unemployment rose from 4.6% in 2007 to 9.6% in 2010 (nearly 10%), the highest since the 1980s, with forecasts implying only a slow decrease in 2011-2012.

Before the crisis China grew at roughly 10% a year; during the crisis growth barely decreased and unemployment barely increased, sustained by a major fiscal expansion (especially public investment) that offset slower exports.

Stock markets fell globally, not just in the U.S.: by end-2008 indexes for the United States, the Euro area and emerging economies had lost half or more of their value from previous peaks (Figure 1-1, January 2007 = 1.0).

No. Okun's law links higher-than-usual output growth to falling unemployment (U.S. slope about -0.4; ~3% growth needed to keep unemployment constant), but it is an average relation, not a guarantee that fast growth always means fewer people out of work.

Even before the crisis Euro-area unemployment averaged 8.5% over 2000-2007 (vs lower U.S. rates), linked to labor-market institutions (firing costs and generous unemployment insurance). After the crisis unemployment rose to about 10% and was forecast to fall only slowly because of low growth.
China kept growing because a major fiscal expansion—especially higher public investment—nearly fully offset the adverse demand effect of slower exports during the crisis.

Banks bundled mortgages into securities that were repackaged into still more complex securities and sold on; when housing prices fell and defaults rose, many banks held securities of uncertain value, froze interbank lending, and amplified the financial crisis.
When housing prices fall, households cut consumption (alongside stock-price declines and uncertainty), reducing demand and output.
A recession is commonly defined as at least two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth, though there is no single official definition and the term is also used more broadly.
